This study investigated the factors affecting self-regulation in learning mathematics with the teacher-promoting interaction, parental support, and the mediating role of math intrinsic motivation. Covariance-based structural equation modeling was employed to examine structural relationships between the variables. A total of 1112 senior high school learners under the Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) strand in Central Visayas, Philippines, participated in the study. The results indicate positive and significant relationships among the five hypothesized paths, leading to self-regulation in learning mathematics as the most endogenous variable. Moreover, the direct relationships between teacher-promoting interaction and parental support to self-regulation in learning mathematics were partially mediated by intrinsic motivation. We put forward three critical insights into self-regulation in mathematics learning: (1) fostering teacher-student interaction boosts intrinsic motivation and self-study, (2) parental support shapes student motivation and self-regulation, and (3) considering the mediation effect of intrinsic motivation on teacher-student interaction and parental support is essential. Policy directions for the STEM curriculum, especially among developing economies, were discussed.

The growing use of communication and information technology (ICT) allows for the improvement of distance learning, at the same time challenging teachers to apply ICT effectively in designing interactive lessons which would involve all students as active participants. Students should be able to monitor themselves by self-regulating and exerting control over their learning, taking responsibility, and directing the process. The aim of the research is to explore students' evaluation of distance learning, as well as the strategies they apply in the learning process, while also determining the connection between their assessment and strategy use. The Student Evaluation of Online Teaching Effectiveness (SEOTE) was used to examine the students' evaluation of online teaching, while the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) was used to examine the use of motivated learning strategies. The results show that students who feel more confident in learning, who set internal goals and are able to self-regulate, evaluate online teaching more positively. Furthermore, students who use cognitive strategies more often rate communication with teachers higher and report spending more time on mastering the content and completing academic assignments. On the other hand, students who experience test anxiety tend to avoid working with peers. These findings imply that students with higher levels of self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, self-regulation, and strategy use give higher rates to the overall quality of online teaching, while anxiety hinders social interaction and joint learning.

Motivation plays a crucial role in learning, particularly when mastering a musical instrument. However, it remains a relatively unexplored area in Hungarian research. In this study, the researchers aim to investigate the relationship between social relations and various aspects of motivation in learning musical instruments, including the motivation to start learning, continue playing, and practice musical instruments regularly. The sample included 264 Hungarian musical instrument students, categorized into three age groups: (1) early adolescents: 9–13-year-olds; (2) mid-adolescents: 14–16-year-olds; (3) late adolescents: 17–19-year-olds. In the course of the cross-sectional data collection, the students filled out the motivation for learning music (MLM) questionnaire, while they were also asked to answer questions about social relationships and demographic data. The MLM questionnaire is based on the five dimensions of self-determination theory: amotivation, external regulation, introjection, identification, and intrinsic motivation. The measurement tool demonstrated reliability across all five dimensions. According to the results, there are significant differences between the age groups in the motivation dimensions, while no gender differences were observed. Based on the regression analysis, social relationships have an impact on learning motivation; however, the role and strength of incentives change with age. For early adolescents, parents exert the greatest influence, whereas teachers and friends play a more significant role for mid-adolescents, and friends become the most decisive influence for late adolescents. The results can be useful for professionals and parents as they can contribute to maintaining motivation.

Public servants’ intrinsic motivation—‘their experience of enjoyment, interest and satisfaction in work’—is an important correlate of performance (Wright 2004; Cerasoli et al. 2014; Sansone & Harackiewicz 2000) and well-being (Ryan & Deci 2000). Conversely, a lack of intrinsic motivation inhibits the creativity (Houtgraaf & Ropes in press; Houtgraaf et al. 2021; Houtgraaf et al. 2023) and productivity (Grant 2008; Becchetti et al. 2013) required to provide the effective, user-centered policies/services that citizens need and demand (Clarke et al. 2007; Van Thiel 2017; Torfing 2016). Furthermore, inadequate motivation diminishes public servants’ experienced wellbeing (Barret-Cheetham et al. 2016; Borst 2018) and is associated with dissatisfaction, boreout, burnout, turnover and part-time work in the public sector (Kim 2018; Borst & Knies 2023; Stazyk et al. 2011). Adequate levels of intrinsic motivation are thus of central importance for both workforce performance, well-being and retention. Meanwhile, both practitioners and academics voice that captivating and retaining public servants is increasingly becoming a challenge—especially with more junior public servants. In general, attracting and retaining an intrinsically motivated workforce appears difficult due to numerous developments in both the nature of work and the nature of employees (Davidesque et al. 2020; Twenge et al. 2010; Cahill et al. 2012). In the public sector too, sustainable employment is of growing concern, illustrated by efforts to understand and safeguard public servants’ well-being, performance and retention (Van der Meer et al. 2022; Borst & Knies 2023; Johari et al. 2019). The challenges of captivating and retaining seems especially true for employees from more recent generations—or at least of younger age (Schröder 2023)—that are argued to have different and more pronounced expectations and preferences relating to work (Waworuntu et al. 2022). In the Netherlands, for example, the translated ‘captivate and bind’ programs sprout throughout the public sector in an alarmed effort to retain (junior) public servants (Binnenlands Bestuur 2024). However, our knowledge regarding intrinsic motivation amidst bureaucratic constraints falls short on two major accounts. Firstly, insight is lacking on whether a lack of intrinsic motivation is an issue in the public sector as a result of bureaucratic constraints and through what mechanisms this would or would not occur. On the one hand, bureaucratic constraints such as formalization and centralization arguably have several negative effects that relate to a lack of intrinsic motivation (Giauque et al. 2012; George et al. 2021; Lavigna 2013; Serhan et al. 2018). On the other hand, such bureaucratic constraints might not lead to amotivation as public servants’ motivation is argued to be a relatively stable concept (Baldwin 1990; Houtgraaf & Ropes in press) and because public servants’ argued idiosyncratic personality may actually lead them to value bureaucratic elements (Leisha & DeHart-Davis 2007; Merton 1940; Bozeman & Rainey 1998). Applying Self-Determination Theory and assessing whether bureaucratic constraints as forms of external locus of control diminish public servants’ sense of autonomy and competence and thereby lead to amotivation (Ryan & Deci 2000, see also Ekval 1996) would provide insight on underlying mechanisms but has not been applied. Secondly, insight is lacking on the role of age/generation, despite evidence pointing towards a significant moderating function. Millennials and more recent generations are argued to assign particular value to elements of autonomy and positive hierarchical feedback relating to competence in their work (Waworuntu et al. 2022), which appears at odds with bureaucratic constraints such as formalization and centralization typically present in the public sector that may stifle such senses of autonomy and competence (Boyne 2002; Bozeman 2000; Ekval 1996). Moreover, recent findings dispute that such differences relating to work motivation and preferences are a result of generational differences but a function of age (Schröder 2023). In short, insight is lacking on whether and why bureaucratic constraints relate to amotivation, what role age/generation plays and thus what strategies and tactics to employ in order to captivate and retain public servants—especially junior ones. Therefore, the goal of this study was to scrutinize whether and how bureaucratic dimensions relate to public servants’ intrinsic motivation whilst paying particular attention to self-determination as an underlying mechanism and the role of age. To these ends, several analyses are conducted on cross-sectional data from 1158 public servants working in a range of Dutch public sector organizations to answer the research question: ‘Through which mechanisms do levels of public servants’ intrinsic motivation correlate with the presence of bureaucratic dimensions, taking into account age?’. Scrutinizing these mechanisms allowed for detailed insights in mechanisms of intrinsic motivation and how to safeguard it in the public sector context, especially among specific age groups. The ensuing results provide public sector practitioners, managers, HR-departments and training organizations with avenues on whether and how to effectively counter adverse effects of bureaucratic dimensions on public servants’ motivation in order to captivate and retain public servants’ and in turn improve their performance, wellbeing and sustainable employment. MOTIVATION AMIDST BUREAUCRATIC CONSTRAINTS Intrinsic motivation and Self-Determination Theory Intrinsic motivation encompasses an experience of enjoyment, interest and satisfaction in work that stems from the employee itself, instead of external factors (Wright 2004; Ryan & Deci 2000; Li et al. 2015). According to Self-Determination Theory, the central characteristic of intrinsic motivation is that it stems from an internal locus of control whereby the individual experiences a control over its own actions and outcomes, instead of an external locus of control whereby the individual experiences that its actions and outcomes are determined by external factors such as managers or rules (Deci & Ryan 1985; Li et al. 2015). In more detail, according to Self-Determination Theory, senses of autonomy, competence and relatedness are essential psychological needs that can be satisfied or frustrated and thus determine the degree of an internal locus of control and experience of intrinsic motivation: the individual has to perceive itself as an autonomous actor that is able and capable of acting in correspondence with its values and goals (Chen et al. 2015; Deci & Ryan 1985). External locus of control, however, may lead to a lack of perceived internal locus of control, hampering intrinsic motivation (Bénabou & Tirole 2003; Deci and Ryan 1985) and leading to amotivation whereby the enjoyment, interest and satisfaction of work becomes increasingly absent (Howard et al., 2016). In general, intrinsic motivation is perceived as beneficial for performance and well-being (Houtgraaf & Ropes in press; Ryan & Deci 2000; Grant 2008; Becchetti et al. 2013), which results in the reasoning that an impairing external locus of control that may hamper employees’ intrinsic motivation ought to be avoided. When assessing intrinsic motivation, it is important to determine whether the concept is approached as an attitude or a state, depending on the goal and timeline of assessment. If considered an attitude, intrinsic motivation is assessed based on an individual’s recall over a longer period of time based on the remembering-self, thereby leading to a more average and stable assessment of the level of intrinsic motivation, whereas if considered a state, intrinsic motivation is assessed on based on an individual’s experience in the current moment based on the experiencing-self, thereby leading to accurate but momentarily and fluctuating assessments of levels of intrinsic motivation (Kahneman & Riis 2005). As the goal of this study concerns assessing how individuals recall their work contexts and attitudes in general and on average in order to assess relations, intrinsic motivation is approached and measured as an attitude in this study (Lee & Choi 2003). Formalization as external locus of control Formalization—the degree to which work related processes and interactions are generally governed by formal rules, standard policies and procedures (Boyne 2002; Bozeman 2000)—can be perceived as representing external locus of control that may hamper public servants’ intrinsic motivation. Formalization is a typical bureaucratic dimension of mechanistic organizations (Brown 2014) and although public sector reforms have aimed at reduction of formalization (Van Thiel 2001), public sector organizations are characterized as featuring at least certain levels of formalization (Borins 2010; Boyne 2002; Boye et al. 2022; Houtgraaf et al. 2023). The object of such bureaucratic principles as expressed in formalization is to achieve stability, standardization and to avoid flexibility and change (Ekval 1996) by controlling employee behavior (Hirst et al. 2009). As such, formalization is a clear example of external locus of control that may hamper intrinsic motivation. Arguably, the underlying mechanisms are twofold. On the one hand, the rules and procedures imposed by formalization may frustrate a sense of autonomy as the individual might not be able to act as it would without these external controls (Hirst et al. 2009). On the other hand, formalization its rules and procedures are related to passive, rule-bound and anxious behavior to stay inside established boundaries (Ekval 1996), which may frustrate a sense of competence as the individual might feel less capable and efficacious in conducting work as a result of the external controls (Au 2015). Science popularization projects have been studied from different points of view and theories.However, little is known about how they can affect the motivation to learn.In the present study, the contribution of interactive lectures to motivation to learn chemistry in public school students was analyzed.Four interactive lectures were developed from the partnership between the authors of the present study as science communicators and different research groups of a public university in Brazil.The lectures were presented in a science museum and in the university to around 150 students of three public schools during one year and were analyzed through the Self-Determination Theory.The Intrinsic Motivation Inventory revealed that the lectures promoted the interest, value of chemistry, effort and perceived choice to the detriment of the sense of pressure to learning chemistry.The interviews also showed that the students became more interested and dedicated in chemistry.The results foment the potential of the interactive lectures for motivation to learn and the responsibility of public universities with science popularization projects.

In this article, we address a form of active perception characterized by curiosity-driven, open-ended exploration with intrinsic motivation, carried out by a group of agents. The multiple agents and a large number of possible actions are the main motivation for incorporating Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning used to train a neural network in order to derive agent’s policy. Partially Observable Markov Decision Process framework is used to accommodate the inaccuracy of sensors and probabilistic nature of agent’s actions. The proposed method incorporates a consensus that derives the common belief vector, thus allowing each agent to make its decisions based on information acquired by all agents involved in the process of active perception. A well-known benchmark problem with a decentralized tiger scenario was used to demonstrate the possibility of the method to generate agents with different perceptual characteristics by simply changing the agents’ reward function related to their intrinsic motivation. The main validation of the proposed approach was performed by using an example of multi-agent search mission. Final results are presented and discussed, and possible avenues for progress on open problems are identified.

Despite the fact that Artificial Intelligence (AI) has boosted the achievement of remarkable results across numerous data analysis tasks, however, this is typically accompanied by a significant shortcoming in the exhibited transparency and trustworthiness of the developed systems. In order to address the latter challenge, the so-called eXplainable AI (XAI) research field has emerged, which aims, among others, at estimating meaningful explanations regarding the employed model’s reasoning process. The current study focuses on systematically analyzing the recent advances in the area of Multimodal XAI (MXAI), which comprises methods that involve multiple modalities in the primary prediction and explanation tasks. In particular, the relevant AI-boosted prediction tasks and publicly available datasets used for learning/evaluating explanations in multimodal scenarios are initially described. Subsequently, a systematic and comprehensive analysis of the MXAI methods of the literature is provided, taking into account the following key criteria: a) The number of the involved modalities (in the employed AI module), b) The processing stage at which explanations are generated, and c) The type of the adopted methodology (i.e. the actual mechanism and mathematical formalization) for producing explanations. Then, a thorough analysis of the metrics used for MXAI methods’ evaluation is performed. Finally, an extensive discussion regarding the current challenges and future research directions is provided.
